title: Every soul tastes death
hook: every soul shall taste death, and the world is the enjoyment of delusion (3:185)

segments.voice: Yesterday, shura: consultation, and a gentleness the Qur'an calls a mercy. Your line was gentle, and consult. Did you ask someone before deciding? Day three hundred seventy-four.

A phone buzzes with bad news: a friend's grandfather has died. In the family chat, the replies come in, prayers for mercy, and then one line in Arabic. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt. Every soul will taste death. To an outsider it can sound blunt, even cold, to send to a grieving family. To the people sending it, it's said gently: this road is everyone's road, and he did not walk it alone. Today, the verse that line comes from.
screen: `BAD NEWS IN THE FAMILY CHAT.` → `ONE LINE IN ARABIC.` → `EVERYONE'S ROAD.`

segments.voice: Al 'Imran 185, in Pickthall's words, begins: "Every soul will taste of death." The same sentence appears in two other surahs as well, 21:35 and 29:57, so this is a line the Qur'an returns to. Notice the verb. Not every soul will die, but every soul will taste death. Dha'iqa, from dhaqa, to taste. Tasting is personal: nobody can taste something for you. And a taste is brief; it isn't the whole meal. Some readers hear a quiet hint in that: death is something the soul goes through, not where it ends. The verse goes on: you'll be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever is drawn away from the Fire and brought into the Garden has truly won. Then it ends, again in Pickthall's words: "The life of this world is but comfort of illusion." The Arabic is mata' al-ghurur. Mata' is provision, things you use for a while, like supplies for a trip. Ghurur is deception, the kind that flatters you into forgetting. The world isn't called evil here. It's called useful, and easy to be fooled by. A hadith in Tirmidhi tells people to remember often the destroyer of pleasures, meaning death. Another, in Bukhari, says: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. The point isn't gloom. Travelers enjoy the road. They just don't forget where they're going.
screen: `THE SAME LINE, THREE TIMES` · `TASTE: PERSONAL, AND PASSING` · `MATA': SUPPLIES FOR A TRIP` · `A STRANGER, OR A TRAVELER` · then, large: `EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle, and you can stop at any point. If you're grieving right now, just breathe and skip ahead. When the bell starts, sit comfortably, and let yourself think, calmly, that your life has an end you don't know the date of. Not with fear. Like a traveler checking the ticket. Then ask one question: if this were a trip, what supplies am I carrying that I won't need, and what am I forgetting to pack? Let one answer come. The bell holds the time.
Dha'iqa, tasting: brief, and personal, not the whole meal. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt, from 3:185, and twice more in the Qur'an. Today's word.

Your line: every soul tastes it. Today, put down one thing you're carrying that won't matter on the last day, a grudge, a worry about looking good, and pack one thing that will. Day three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Muslims recite 'every soul will taste death' at funerals, in condolences and in sermons, and it is sometimes carved on gravestones; remembering death is encouraged as a way to live with purpose, not in fear.

fork.setup: the hadith says to be in this world in a certain way. which one?
options: as a king in his palace.
as a stranger, or a traveler passing through.
as a monk who owns nothing.
fork.reveal: a stranger or a traveler (Bukhari): someone who uses the road and enjoys it, but doesn't forget where they're going.

original.note: Arabic: every soul will taste death (3:185; also 21:35, 29:57).

trapdoor: what you thought: a grim reminder.
what it means: death is certain and personal, and the world is provision for a journey, not the destination.
what a scholar hears: dha'iqa, tasting, read by some as death being passed through rather than an ending; mata' al-ghurur, provision that deceives.
